title: The place
subtitle: In the rain shadow of the Vosges
objectives: Explain its French and German history

steps.title: A narrow strip
steps.body: Alsace lies in north-east France, a narrow strip about 120 km long between the Vosges mountains to the west and the Rhine river to the east, on the border with Germany. Vineyards run along the lower slopes of the Vosges, from 200 to 450 m. Soils are a mosaic: granite, limestone, schist, sandstone, volcanic and marl.

steps.title: Rain shadow
steps.body: The Vosges block wet westerly winds, so Alsace is one of France's driest regions; Colmar gets only about 500 mm of rain a year. Summers are warm and sunny, autumns long and dry. That lets grapes ripen fully in a northern latitude, around 48 degrees, giving ripe, aromatic wines with good acidity.

steps.prompt: Why is Alsace so dry and sunny for its latitude?
options: The Vosges block rain from the west
steps.explanation: The mountains cast a rain shadow.

steps.title: Between two countries
steps.body: Alsace changed hands between France and Germany several times: German from 1871 to 1918, and occupied again in 1940 to 1944. Its culture, architecture and grape names show both influences. It uses the tall, slim flûte bottle, required by law, and names grapes on labels, unlike most of France.

steps.explanation: Blending 13 grapes is a southern Rhône practice.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Alsace lies between the Vosges and the Rhine
The Vosges rain shadow makes it dry and sunny
Its French and German history shows in labels and bottles
